title: I'll Sleep When I'm Dead
full_review:
British actor Clive Owen and director Mike Hodges reunite after their sleeper hit, "Croupier," in the moody suspense film "I'll Sleep When I'm Dead" (Paramount Classics), set against a backdrop of London's seedy criminal underworld.
Davey (Jonathan Rhys Meyers), a young man dabbling in drug-dealing among the beautiful set as well as other petty criminal activities, is grabbed off the street after a night on the town and brutally raped by the villainous Boad (Malcolm McDowall). In his despair, he returns home in a state of shock, lies for hours in a tub of water and slits his throat. None of his friends can understand the motives for his despairing action.
Meanwhile, his older brother, Will Graham (Clive Owen), a former underworld character now living an almost hermitical life in a trailer in the forest, learns of his death and is drawn back to London to uncover the motives behind the seemingly senseless suicide. Along the way, he encounters his old flame (Charlotte Rampling) and a former crony (Jamie Foreman).

This is an unpleasant story and milieu that will repel many viewers but, in fairness, the characters are not glamorized and there's actually very little overt violence, in spite of the criminal underworld setting and heavy air of menace that pervades the film.

Superb British actor Owen is quite sympathetic in his powerfully taciturn way, and you can really feel his conflict as he tries to suppress his desire for revenge of his beloved brother while resisting going back to his criminal ways. Rampling's character, equally enigmatic, registers as a strong screen presence as she first rebuffs Will after his abandonment years before, then encourages him not to backslide.

Jamie Foreman as Davey's best friend, distraught at his death, is likeably sympathetic, as is veteran actress Sylvia Syms as a warmhearted landlady. McDowell (playing one of his trademark baddies) is appropriately, if rather conventionally, hateful. Ken Stott as an underworld character out to get Will projects the requisite air of menace.

The story is as sordid as they come, but Will's character -- unloved, always on the move, trusting no one -- is a morally complex character. He knows he's come to his present state out of "grief for a life wasted." And his obsession about Davey's death is partly in recognition of Davey's existence having been "another wasted life." The film shows that, try as he may, Will cannot escape his past. Or can he? Hodges is on record as saying the film is about "man's constant attempt to climb out of the slime."

Toward the film's end, Trevor Preston's script gets bogged down in pedantic descriptions of the causes and effects of rape, dumbing down to the banality of an average television police drama, but the writing is, on the whole, above average. The ending could be construed as unsatisfying in its moral ambiguity.
All in all, Hodges skillfully maintains the somber and suspenseful mood, though the plot at first seems a bit hard to follow, as viewers struggle to connect the disparate elements. So, too, the regional accents make for some unintelligibility. Still, for those not turned off by the squalid story, this is an absorbing if flawed tale.

Because of a discreetly brief rape scene, fleeting rear nudity, some recreational drug abuse, a crass scene involving urination and some rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
